_source: Nghiem & Daume, SMARTER: A Data-efficient Framework to Improve Toxicity Detection with Explanation via Self-augmenting Large Language Models, ACL 2026 (long), https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.1584/. Instruction sentence verbatim from Figure 6 (p. 34324, the paper's classification prompt without explanation; the repo's CLS_PROMPT_NO_EXP in Code/utils/prompt_templates.py @3489b7e), with {categories} filled as the repo's format_label_block does (labels joined by ', ' in Table 4 order); the 'Provide your response in the following format' line is dropped because Jev answers in a typed choice. Label names from Table 4 (p. 34320). Criteria quote the Table 10 definitions (p. 34328, 'collected from their original publications') verbatim, prefixed by the Table 10 category name; only PDF line-break hyphenation and typographic quotes are normalised. The state sentence is ours (describes the HateXplain release format).

question.instructions: By considering their corresponding Definitions, label the following post with only one of these categories: Normal, Offensive, Hate. The state holds one social media post ("post") from Gab or Twitter, as released in HateXplain: lowercased and tokenised, with placeholders such as <user> and <number>.

criteria.Normal: Normal: neither hate speech nor offensive.
criteria.Offensive: Offensive Language: usage of rude, hurtful, derogatory, obscene or insulting language to upset or embarrass people.
criteria.Hate: Hate Speech: language which attacks, demeans, offends, threatens, or insults a group based on race, ethnic origin, religion, disability, gender, age, sexual orientation, or other traits. it is not the presence of certain words that makes the text hate speech, rather you should look the context the word is used in the text.
